Recording 9: Mono and Stereo

Stereo pairs, one earbud and summing to mono, live sound, speaker placement, laptops and two subwoofers.

A mono signal is one channel: one microphone, one cable, one speaker or many speakers all playing the same thing. A stereo signal is two channels, left and right, that differ a little, and the differences are what put sounds somewhere between the speakers (Sound 23: Stereo). Most music is recorded largely in mono, mixed into stereo, and then heard, quite often, back in mono. Each step has its traps.

Recording: mostly mono

  • One source, one mic is a mono track: vocal, bass DI, kick, snare, guitar amp. That isn’t a weakness: the mix places each mono track in the stereo picture with the pan knob. A “stereo” vocal is almost never wanted.
  • Two mics on one source is not automatically stereo. Two mics at different distances on a guitar amp hear the same sound at slightly different times; mixed together they comb-filter (cancel some frequencies, boost others). Check the polarity button and nudge the far track in time until the low end is fullest. The 3:1 rule helps: the second mic at least three times as far from the first as the first is from its source.
  • Stereo pairs record space on purpose (Recording 2: Microphones):
    • XY: two cardioids, capsules touching at 90–135°. Only level differences, no time differences, so it sums to mono cleanly. Narrower image.
    • ORTF / spaced pair (AB): capsules apart. Time differences give a wide, airy image, but in mono the delays comb-filter: the more spaced, the more it can go hollow.
    • Mid/side: a forward mic (mid) and a sideways figure-8 (side), decoded to L = M + S, R = M − S. In mono the side cancels exactly and you get the mid mic, perfectly. Width is adjustable after the fact.
  • Stereo sources: keyboards, synths and drum machines often come out stereo (L/R outputs). Record both if the patch is really stereo (a chorus, a Leslie, a stereo piano sample); record one if the two sides are identical.
  • Room and overhead mics are where stereo recording matters most: the drum kit, the choir, the piano, the hall.

Mixing: building the stereo picture

The mixing rules all serve two listeners at once, the one on stereo speakers and the one in mono:

  • Centre the things that carry the song: kick, snare, bass, lead vocal. A centred (mono) sound is equal in both channels, so it survives every playback system, and its bass energy is shared by both speakers.
  • Pan the rest. Pan is a level difference; it sums to mono without cancelling.
  • Pan law: a sound panned centre plays in both speakers; to sound as loud as when it’s hard to one side, the centre is turned down 3 dB (or 4.5 or 6, the DAW decides). When the mix folds to mono, centre sounds come up relative to hard-panned ones, so a balance can shift a little.
  • Wideners (Haas delays, phase tricks, stereo chorus, some “stereo enhancer” plug-ins) make width out of time and phase differences, and those are exactly what cancel in mono.
  • Double-tracking (playing the part twice, panned left and right) is the safe way to wide: the two takes differ naturally, so in mono they just sound like two players, not a comb filter.

One earbud: what happens when stereo is summed to mono

Take one earbud out and the other still plays one channel only: you’d hear the left side of the mix, missing whatever was panned hard right (the second guitar, half the drum kit, a backing vocal). That’s why phones and operating systems have a Mono Audio setting (iOS: Accessibility → Audio & Visual; Android, macOS and Windows have one too), and many earbuds switch to mono by themselves when only one is in. A single Bluetooth speaker, a phone’s speaker, a smart speaker, a shop’s ceiling speakers and many club and church PAs do the same thing: they play L + R (usually scaled by ½, or −3 dB, to keep it from clipping).

What summing does to a mix:

  • Anything equal in both channels (the centred vocal, kick, bass) adds up and comes through solid. In fact it gets louder relative to the sides (up to 6 dB on a plain L + R, 3 dB with a pan-law sum), so a mono mix sounds more vocal-and-bass heavy.
  • Hard-panned parts stay, at their own level. Nothing is lost, but they drop back relative to the centre.
  • Anything that’s different in the two channels only by timing or phase cancels partly or completely:
    • A Haas widener (the same part a few ms late on one side) becomes a comb filter: hollow, thin, phasey.
    • Out-of-polarity content (one side inverted, often from a miswired mic, a cable, or an overenthusiastic widener) disappears entirely. Instruments or reverb vanish.
    • Spaced-pair overheads and room mics go hollow; the cymbals can swish.
    • Stereo reverb loses much of its tail (a reverb’s two sides are deliberately decorrelated), so a mono mix sounds drier than you meant.
    • Very wide synths and pads (detuned unison spread across the field, stereo chorus) shrink, thin out, and sometimes almost vanish behind the vocal.
    • The side of a mid/side signal is gone: at 200% width you were only turning up what mono throws away.
  • Bass is the worst place for any of this: a bass note slightly out of phase between the sides loses its weight in mono, and a mono subwoofer (see below) gets exactly that cancelled version.

How to check it: press the DAW’s Mono button (or put a utility plug-in on the master set to mono) several times while mixing, and watch a correlation meter or vectorscope. +1 is mono, 0 is wide and unrelated, anything heading toward −1 is trouble. Try it on the widget in Sound 23: Haas delay at 1, 3, 5, 10 ms with Mono on. If a part disappears in mono, fix the source: narrow the widener, use a real double, flip a polarity, or keep the low end (below about 120–150 Hz) mono with a mid/side EQ or a “mono bass” utility.

Live sound

Most of a live audience doesn’t hear stereo. Stereo needs you to sit between the speakers, roughly as far from each, and on a festival field or in a bar almost everyone is much nearer one stack than the other: they hear that side, plus a late copy of the other. So:

  • Many live mixes are mono, or nearly: both sides of the PA play the same mix, and nothing important is panned. If a hard-left guitar plays only from the left stack, the people on the right don’t get the guitar.
  • Stereo is used lightly: reverbs and delays, a little spread on keyboards and overheads, panning a few degrees.
  • Front fills, delay towers and side fills cover the parts of the room the main speakers miss. Delay speakers are delayed to arrive just after the main PA (Haas again, 5–20 ms) so the sound still seems to come from the stage.
  • Monitors (wedges and in-ears) are separate mixes for each player (Recording 6). In-ears are often stereo, for comfort and a sense of the band; wedges are mono.
  • Feedback: a mic in front of a speaker playing it howls. Keep mics behind the main PA, wedges in the mic’s dead zone (behind a cardioid, at the sides of a supercardioid).

Studio listening and speaker placement

In the studio you’re the one listener in the right seat, so stereo works fully, if the room and speakers allow it:

  • Equilateral triangle: the two speakers and your head at its three corners, 1–2 m on a side, tweeters at ear height, speakers angled to point at (or just behind) your head. The phantom centre (a centred vocal floating between them) is the test: if it’s blurred or pulled to one side, the triangle is off.
  • Symmetry: the same distance from each side wall, so both sides reflect alike. Put the desk along the short wall, firing down the room’s long dimension.
  • Off the walls: a speaker near the wall behind it gets extra bass (and a dip where its reflection cancels). Either keep it a metre or more out, or push it nearly flush and use the speaker’s “boundary” EQ switch. Avoid the room’s exact centre (between front and back walls): bass standing waves are worst there.
  • Decouple: stands or isolation pads, not a resonant desk; the desk surface also reflects into your ears.
  • First reflections: absorbers on the side walls (where a mirror would show you the speaker) and above.
  • Level: moderate, ~75–85 dB SPL, then checked quiet.

Laptops, phones and small speakers

  • Laptop speakers are tiny and a few centimetres apart: almost no stereo width (some laptops fake it with processing), and almost nothing below 150–200 Hz. Phones are often one speaker, or two that sum to near-mono.
  • Your bass line has to be heard through its harmonics: a bass with some upper-mid character (pick attack, a little saturation, 700 Hz–1.5 kHz) stays audible; a pure sub-bass sine disappears.
  • Check mixes on the laptop and a phone, in mono. If the vocal is clear, the bass line can be followed and nothing has vanished, the mix translates.
  • Laptop headphone outputs are usually fine; built-in microphones are mono, noisy, and processed (noise suppression, echo cancellation): not for recording music if anything else is available.

Subwoofers, and why two

A subwoofer plays only the deep bass (below a crossover, often 80 Hz). Low frequencies are hard to locate by ear, so one subwoofer is usually fed a mono sum of L + R. That’s another mono fold: any bass that cancels in mono cancels in the sub.

  • Why two? Not mainly for stereo bass (below about 80 Hz you can hardly tell where it comes from). The reason is the room. Bass wavelengths (4 m at 80 Hz, 17 m at 20 Hz) are the size of the room, so the room sets up standing waves: at some seats a note booms, at others it nearly vanishes. Two subs in different places excite those modes differently and fill in each other’s holes, so the bass is even across more seats (and each sub works less hard, with more headroom).
  • Placement: studies (Todd Welti and Allan Devantier at Harman) found two subs at the midpoints of opposite walls, or four at the midpoints of all four, smooth the bass best across a listening area. A corner gives the most level and the most uneven bass.
  • Phase and time: two subs must arrive together at the listener. Use each sub’s phase (0/180° or a dial) and delay so the bass gets louder at the crossover, not thinner; a sub out of phase with the mains causes the same cancellation as an out-of-phase stereo pair.
  • Live, subs are often in a cardioid arrangement (one turned backward and delayed) to keep bass off the stage, or spread across the front in an end-fire or arc. Two stacks far apart, left and right, with the same signal, make a bass power alley down the middle and dead spots in between: the same comb filter as a Haas delay, but a room-sized one.
  • Studio: the sub level is set so it continues the mains smoothly, not as an effect. A mix made with a loud sub will be bass-light everywhere else.

Checklist

  • Kick, bass, snare, lead vocal centred; low end (below ~120 Hz) mono.
  • Mono button pressed often; correlation meter mostly positive.
  • No part disappears in mono; wideners and polarity checked.
  • Checked on speakers, headphones, one earbud, a laptop and a phone.
  • Speakers in a symmetrical triangle; sub(s) in phase with the mains.
